tweets.text: Anthony Davis is up for a Max contract as of today. Please Will Dawkins, stay strong, stay the course, trust your process -- and do not give AD a max contract. Period. The Wizards do not owe Anthony Davis a dollar more than they already owe him. I am thrilled about AD but he is not a free agent and needs to stop acting like one. The résumé is real: ten All-Star teams, a ring, one of the great two-way bigs of his era. The availability is not. 71 games in two seasons. Trae Young was everywhere wearing a custom made Wizards jacket, shirt, etc. Trae was on it and leaning in. You could feel his excitement -- his presence was electric. (I get it, Trae has a contract, but his commitment was still so sincere and refreshing.) Yes, AD showed up (and reportedly participated in the optional minicamp) but, to me, he seemed more to be auditioning for other teams, and not as a Wizard. AD acted like he was undecided, could care less about our community, unsure and all alone -- that was painful to watch. Like I said above, AD acts as if he is a free agent -- and that is just plain wrong. Hey AD: Is it really that challenging to at least seem a little like you are part of our team???!!! Supermax contracts do not work out for the Wiz (Otto, Brad, even John (who was the best of the best) all went poorly after signing). tweets.text: RT @freddienew: My parents died suddenly in a car accident 25 years ago this year. I was 21, and became a guardian for my little brother and sister (10 and 12 at the time). I've spoken about the accident and its impact on a couple of podcasts, but it's fresh on my mind as my brother just shared with me a handwritten letter I sent to him at his school. He's kept it with him ever since. I've transcribed it below; he told me last night that it's helped him many times over the past two decades. Sharing it here in case what I said back then in an attempt to help a little lost boy is of assistance to anyone else. 23 July 2002 To Harry, From Freddie. 1. Don't panic. 2. You have many people watching your back. I am one of them and I am watching it very closely. 3. The accident was nobody's fault. Therefore we cannot legitimately blame anyone for it. We call it an accident for this reason. 4. We cannot bring Mummy and Daddy back – but this has important consequences: – We need to remember what they taught us. – We need to behave as they would have wanted us to. – Because they are not alive, but we are, we owe both ourselves and their memory a duty to live as well and as fully as we possibly can, not to give in, not to give up. Because of the accident we have been given a very special insight into what it means to be alive – to live as fully as we can, to consider others, to work at what we are good at, and work even harder at what is difficult. Something has been wasted, something has been lost. We must make sure that our lives are not. We shall always regret that Mummy and Daddy are not here – let us not regret anything we do, or know that we had a chance and threw it away. Whatever happens, I have got your back. Even if I do sometimes hit you with cricket balls. Run straight, look your foe in the eye, and never back down. Strength and honour! I love you very much.

"With a discretionary multi-protocol vault you have two new truths to secure that math can no longer give you: is the attested price honest, and is the strategist actually allowed to do the thing they just did with the funds. BoringVault, built by Veda Labs, is the cleanest answer the industry has to those two questions, and its design is worth studying line by line because it is what a serious vault looks like in 2026. The core BoringVault contract is deliberately boring, it is roughly a hundred lines that do nothing but hold the assets and mint or burn shares. tweets.text: RT @auryn_macmillan: I'll probably get crucified for this, but it seems a large part of the tension in the ETH issuance rate wanting rates to be high enough to justify solo/small staking operations while not overpaying/hurting security because large/liquid staking providers pile in on those rates. Cutting rates hurts security because it makes solo/small staking operators less viable. Maintaining current rates eventually hurts security because too large of a percentage of stake accumulates in a very small number of large staking operators. The solution to this is to give smaller stakers better rates / have diminishing returns for ever larger stakes. The issue with this is that it requires some sybil resistance mechanism and there are none that are both reliable at this scale and credibly neutral. @BrightIDProject's Auroa still seems like the closest thing to a solution that would be viable for something like this. But I struggle to see a scenario where a critical mass of staking weight gets behind something like this, in part because it means greatly reduced staking yield for large incumbents.

tweets.text: I should be doing other things but couldn’t help myself. What's actually inside Russia’s crypto market structure law? It’s nowhere near as comprehensive as Clarity. But it does some things. It's also very Russian. (Ironically, the law shares some similarities to Canada’s approach.) 1. At a high level, the goal is twofold: enable cross-border trade and ensure domestic licensing. 2 (a). It maintains a ban on using crypto to pay for goods and services in Russia. Carve-outs cover foreign trade settlement, receipts of mined crypto (e.g. Bitcoin), network fees and various securities and digital rights settlements. Exporters and importers will be permitted to use crypto (including stablecoins) in cross-border payments without limitations. 2 (b). It creates a licensing regime for centralized exchanges, requiring operators to be licensed by July 1, 2027. 3. (a) Retail access is capped. "Non-qualified" investors can buy the "most liquid" crypto up to about $3,800 per year per intermediary, a cap set by the Bank of Russia. Qualified investors have no cap. (That cap is per platform, not necessarily per person. Canada took a similar approach, suggesting the concern is more about counterparty risk than digital asset-related risk.) 3. (b) What qualifies as "most liquid"? I hadn't seen this reported anywhere and so I found the actual law and had Claude translate it. Article 31(13) says they may admit an asset only if it has: A. Two-year average market cap above 5 trillion rubles (~$62B) B. Two-year average daily volume above 1 trillion rubles (~$12.5B) C. Five years of published closing prices from a licensed foreign venue doing at least 100 billion rubles in average volume Oof. That's BTC but not much more. Maybe ETH. 4. Crypto is recognized as property. I'm guessing that wasn't always the case and probably has to do with seizure rights. 5. An entity custodying your crypto can only release it to an unhosted address in listed cases.* *Three groups get unrestricted withdrawals: exporters and importers, licensed firms and miners. Everyone else can only withdraw to another regulated custodian (not self-custody). 6. Two points strike me as uniquely Russian: (A) The law prohibits informing residents about how to transact outside this regime, or providing software that lets them. A market structure rule that regulates speech! (B) The government may establish a special regime for crypto circulation that differs from this entire framework, to "protect the constitutional order, economic interests, defense or state security." So it's them saying "Here are the rules. We can change them whenever we need to." lol. glad I wasn't born there.

tweets.text: Longer thread on why 'legitimate' crypto use cases never take off. Lets imagine a real use case of crypto built around social participation in a common enterprise. For this example, lets assume a communal dog-walking platform is a legitimately wholesome and workable enterprise. Adam creates DogeWalk, a fun application for dogowners and dog lovers around the world to connect and dog lovers can sign up to walk the dogs of the dogowners. In order to maintain trust but anonymity amongst the participants, Adam decides to incorporate crypto into DogeWalk, allowing crypto payments and Walk points, a reputation system which supports the legitimacy of the participant. DogeWalk takes off amongst a community of dogwalkers. Turns out that there is legitimate demand for people to walk dogs in an anonymous manner. Adam makes some money from platform fees charged on his some 1,000 users. Bob sees DogeWalk taking off and sees an opportunity. He creates PupStroll as a competitor to DogeWalk and informs the PupStroll users that they can get a piece of PupStroll! Instead of giving all the fees to Adam, together they can share in the decentralized ownership of a dog walking platform! PupStroll is almost exactly like DogeWalk, except PupStroll users get Stroll points, and a referral link. DogeWalk users start moving to PupStroll. PupStroll does a token launch and suddenly everyone is talking about how the future of dog walking is decentralized. People who have never walked a dog in their lives start signing up with PupStroll to walk dogs and farm season 2 of the STROLL airdrop. Charlie sees PupStroll take off and trade at an implied FDV of 20m with 5,000 users. He raises $500,000 from a venture capital fund BrandName Capital by selling 10% of the future supply of HoundTrek. HoundTrek is almost exactly like PupStroll except it has a slightly cooler 'dark mode' UI. Charlie proudly announces his funding round and launches an aggressive points and referral programme. He even provides zero fees and bonus payments, funded from BrandName Capital's investment. PupStroll's users start moving over to HoundTrek given the economic incentives. The price of STROLL declines and angry purchasers of STROLL begin yelling at Bob for not keeping up with HoundTrek. Bob simply does not have the firepower to match. PupStroll's users give up on season 2. HoundTrek announces a second funding round right before TGE, led by DarkArts Capital. DarkArts Capital purchases another 10% of TREK allegedly at a valuation of $20,000,000 but really at a valuation of $10,000,000. HoundTrek launches the TREK token which opens at 25m FDV alongside a small airdrop. The TREK token climbs steadily upward for a while as Charlie uses the funds raised to provide price support while paying for marketing. When the token reaches 100m FDV, DarkArts Capital and BrandName Capital take profit on the token. Number goes down. Everyone gets mad at BrandName Capital and DarkArts Capital. David who sees all these play out, realizes that there is an opportunity. "Tis all the fault of the greedy venture capital funds!" he says. We need "true community ownership!" With that, he opens a funding round for WanderPooch via an 'ICO', valuing WanderPooch at 'only 10m'. He raises 2m of capital. David knows nothing about dogs nor dogwalking platforms. He simply pays himself the money and shuts down the project after a year. Eugene is a former venture capital hotshot. He pulls together a coalition of his VC friends and raises 10m at a 100m valuation to break the dogwalking industry once and for all. CanineHike is the cleanest dogwalking application ever, and in order to generate demand on both sides, he even invests the money into cute dogs for dogwalkers to walk! He pays ever KOL that was early to PupStroll, promising them both money and tokens for writing long threads on why decentralized dogwalking will work this time. To increase platform metrics, Eugene even pays an agency which hires homeless people to walk dogs on CanineHike! Eugene doesn't even like dogs but the marketing works. On TGE, the token trades at 1bn FDV through clever supply control, marketing and a limited airdrop. Eugene dangles a season 2, while amplifying those who made life changing money farming the airdrop. Meanwhile him and his VC friends sell locked tokens at a 60% discount on secondaries. Within 6 months, the HIKE token declines in price. And at the end of it all, decentralised dog walking is decried as a scam by retail users who do not like dogs as they scream at builders who do not like dogs who have been funded by investors who do not like dogs. As for Adam and the people that actually wanted to walk dogs? Yeah they just do it between themselves in hobbyist groups now and will never touch crypto again.

tweets.text: RT @hostis_black: Four senators want every phone and computer sold in America to demand your date of birth before it will work for you. A Linux developer has already published the script that tears it out, under his real name, with an invitation to sue him. The bill is S. 5090, filed July 22 by Andy Kim, Cynthia Lummis, Adam Schiff, and John Barrasso. Two Democrats and two Republicans. It puts an age prompt inside the setup of every operating system in the country. A covered device is any general-purpose computer, so this reaches the phone in your pocket, the laptop on your desk, the console under your television. Accounts you already hold get swept in the day it takes effect. Your own machine then informs on you. It hands your age bracket to every app, every app store, and every browser, and they are required to treat that signal as the primary indicator of who you are. A browser provider under this bill is anyone who owns or maintains a browser. A man maintaining a fork in his spare time carries the same duty as Google, and the fines run $2,500 for a negligent violation and $7,500 for an intentional one, multiplied by every child affected. Section 10 promises no government ID and no face scans. Section 3(d) then says that when a provider gets clear and convincing information that your declared age is wrong, it shall verify. It never says how. Section 4(c) makes app developers report you upstream when they decide you lied. The brackets stop at 17 and file teenagers in with adults, while the state laws this is built to serve draw their line at 18. The federal signal cannot tell a 17 year old from a grown man. Every site under an 18+ mandate will need more than the signal. It will need your papers. The work has already started inside your machine. On March 18 systemd merged a birthDate field into user records, citing California, Colorado, and Brazil by name. systemd runs as the init system on nearly every major distribution, so that field is sitting on Linux boxes whose owners have never heard of any of these bills. Nobody asked you. Nobody is going to. @GrapheneOS answered in March. It will not implement age or identity verification, and if that means its phones cannot be sold in your state, so be it. John McCardle built Ageless Linux. He declared himself in "full, knowing, and intentional noncompliance" with the California statute, cited the section number himself, and invited the lawsuit. His script makes the user the distributor. The liability scatters across every machine that runs it. There is no one man left to drag into court. The script strips the systemd birthDate field and leaves a refusal notice where it stood. If any distribution ever ships a working age daemon, the project has already promised a replacement that answers every query with "unknown." Artix refuses. Devuan refuses. DB48X, an open source calculator firmware, filed a legal notice saying it "does not, cannot and will not implement age verification." A calculator had to publish a legal notice. That is the reach of what these four wrote. S. 5090 takes effect 18 months after it passes, if it passes. The script already works. Take a copy.
